_work.title: Zād al-ashrāf fī wafq al-qāf — Treatise on the Letter Qāf and Its Wafq (Princeton, Garrett no. 335L)
_work.blurb: A short Arabic manuscript treatise in five chapters on the magical properties of the letter qāf (ق) and its use in wafq (magic squares) and charms, 10 leaves (20 pages), 19th century, held at Princeton University Library (Garrett no. 335L). The work is attributed to Ibrāhīm ibn Aḥmad al-Khaṭṭāṭ (the Calligrapher, 18th century). 'Ilm al-qāf — the science of the letter qaf — is a specialized branch of Arabic lettrism focusing on the 21st letter of the Arabic alphabet, whose abjad value is 100 and which occupies a particular position in the cosmological letter-science system: it is associated with the mountains that surround the world (Jabal Qaf, the cosmic mountain range in Islamic cosmology), with specific divine names, and with particular operative applications in talismanic practice. The treatise contains embedded wafq diagrams throughout: a 5×5 numeric magic square of the letter qaf, a 5×5 letter-arrangement wafq, a property/attribute table correlating the letter qaf's correspondences, and most spectacularly, a full-page labeled jadwal — the 'first of sixteen jadwal tables' (al-jadwal al-awwal min al-sita 'ashar jadwalan) — a large rectangular numeric grid occupying nearly the full page. The MS is written in naskh script with red ink used for chapter headings, emphasis, and the numerals/letters within the wafq cells.
_work.rights: Public Domain — 19th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
_work.creator: Khaṭṭāṭ, Ibrāhīm ibn Aḥmad (18th century)

entries.title: Wafq al-Qaf — Numeric and Letter Magic Squares (Zad al-ashraf, f. 3a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A page from the Zad al-ashraf fi wafq al-qaf (Princeton Garrett 335L) showing two embedded wafq magic square diagrams within Arabic text. In the upper-right section: a bordered 5×5 numeric magic square with red Arabic numerals in each cell — the standard 25-cell wafq with numbers summing to a constant in each row, column, and diagonal, here associated with the letter qaf (abjad value 100; the 5×5 qaf wafq will have rows summing to a value keyed to 100). In the lower-right section: a second bordered 5×5 grid containing Arabic letter combinations rather than numerals — a letter-arrangement wafq in which the cells encode specific divine names or letter combinations derived from the letter qaf and its associated cosmic correspondences. The surrounding Arabic text (in the chapter heading and body) explicitly names these figures as 'wafq al-qaf' and discusses their construction and operative use. The text running diagonally at the bottom margin contains additional charm instructions (in the margins and between the grid and the bottom of the page). This folio demonstrates the characteristic format of Islamic lettrism manuscripts: prose explanation alternating with operative diagrams on the same page, where the diagrams are simultaneously mathematical objects and talismanic forms.

entries.title: Wafq al-Qaf — 5×5 Numeric Magic Square Embedded in Text (Zad al-ashraf, f. 3b)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A text page from the Zad al-ashraf fi wafq al-qaf (Princeton Garrett 335L) with a 5×5 numeric magic square in the lower-right portion of the page, embedded within the running text. The wafq grid has a double red-ink border and contains red Arabic numerals in 25 cells. This is the operative wafq for the letter qaf — either a 5×5 Martian square (Mars is the planet associated with qaf in some traditions, with the 5×5 grid summing to 65) or a specifically computed qaf-wafq whose construction is explained in the surrounding text. The text on this folio discusses the mystical properties of the letter qaf — its 'wajha' (faces/aspects), its celestial correspondences, and the conditions for using its wafq. In Islamic lettrism, each of the 28 Arabic letters has a specific wafq associated with it; the qaf-wafq is among the most powerful because of qaf's cosmic significance (Jabal Qaf, the world-mountain) and its high abjad value (100, a perfect round number). The page heading in red ink identifies this as part of Chapter 3 (fasl al-thalith) of the treatise.

entries.title: Al-Jadwal al-Awwal — First of Sixteen Jadwal Tables, Large Numeric Grid (Zad al-ashraf, f. 4a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A spectacular full-page numeric jadwal (table) from the Zad al-ashraf fi wafq al-qaf (Princeton Garrett 335L), labeled at the top 'al-jadwal al-awwal min al-sita 'ashar jadwalan' (The First of the Sixteen Jadwal Tables). The grid occupies most of the page and contains rows and columns of red Arabic numerals, with the grid ruled in black ink. The 16 jadwal system is a technique for expanding a basic wafq into 16 variant configurations — each derived by a specific systematic transformation (rotation, reflection, digit-manipulation) of the base magic square. In the qaf tradition, the 16 jadwal tables represent the 16 different operative configurations of the qaf-wafq, each corresponding to a different magical purpose or planetary hour. The sheer scale of this jadwal page (16 complete numeric grids are represented across a set of pages in this treatise) demonstrates the computational ambition of the 'ilm al-qaf system — the practitioner is not merely copying a single magic square but has access to the full 16-configuration system for maximum precision in talisman construction. The page below the large grid contains a short explanatory text identifying the tables and their uses.

entries.title: Qaf Property Table, Numeric Wafq, and Letter Wafq (Zad al-ashraf, f. 4b)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A page from the Zad al-ashraf fi wafq al-qaf (Princeton Garrett 335L) containing three distinct diagrammatic elements: (1) At the top: a bordered property/attribute table with labeled rows and columns correlating the letter qaf's attributional correspondences — planets, elements, humors, mansions, times, colors, names — in the standard Islamic letter-science jadwal format for systematic attribute lookup. (2) At lower left: a 5×5 numeric magic square (wafq) with red Arabic numerals — a variant configuration of the qaf-wafq (possibly from the 16-jadwal system represented on the facing folio). (3) At lower right: a 5×5 letter wafq with Arabic letters in each cell — a letter-arrangement magic square encoding specific letter combinations derived from the letter qaf's associations. The presence of all three table types on a single page — attribute-lookup table, numeric magic square, and letter magic square — demonstrates the systematic layering of information in Islamic lettrism practice: the attribute table tells the practitioner which correspondences apply; the numeric wafq provides the mathematical structure; and the letter wafq provides the operative text for inscription on a talisman.
